cards.q: In physiology, what does a 1 molar (1 M) solution contain?
cards.a: One mole of solute dissolved in enough water to make one liter of final solution.
options: One mole of solute per liter of final solution
One mole of solute per kilogram of water
One osmole of dissolved particles per liter of solution
One gram of solute per liter of final solution
cards.explanation: Molarity counts moles of solute in a liter of finished solution, so you dissolve the solute and then bring the total volume up to one liter. Moles per kilogram of water is molality, a unit physiology rarely uses because volumes, not water masses, are what we measure. Osmoles per liter is osmolarity, which counts particles after dissociation rather than moles of the original compound. Grams per liter is a mass concentration and ignores molar mass entirely.

cards.q: Osmolarity measures which quantity in a solution?
cards.a: The total number of dissolved particles per liter of solution.
options: The mass of solute in grams per liter of solution
The number of molecules of one named solute per liter
The total number of dissolved particles per liter of solution
The fraction of dissolved particles that cannot cross the membrane
cards.explanation: Osmolarity is a particle count, which is why 1 mmol/L of NaCl contributes 2 mOsm/L while 1 mmol/L of glucose contributes only 1 mOsm/L. Grams per liter is a mass concentration and says nothing about particle number. Counting one named solute gives you that solute's molarity, not the osmolarity of the whole solution. Whether particles can cross the membrane is the question tonicity answers, and that is a separate idea from osmolarity.

cards.q: What is normal plasma osmolarity in a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 290 mOsm/L.
options: About 150 mOsm/L
About 290 mOsm/L
About 450 mOsm/L
About 900 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Plasma runs in a tight band near 285 to 295 mOsm/L, and the body defends that range with thirst and antidiuretic hormone. About 150 is the plasma sodium concentration in mEq/L, and sodium plus its accompanying anions accounts for roughly twice that in osmolarity. 450 and 900 mOsm/L are values you find deep in the renal medulla during concentration of urine, not in circulating plasma.

cards.q: What does a milliequivalent (mEq) account for that a millimole does not?
cards.a: The electrical charge the ion carries.
options: The mass of the ion in milligrams
The osmotic pull the ion exerts across a membrane
The speed at which the ion moves through a channel
The electrical charge the ion carries
cards.explanation: Milliequivalents are millimoles multiplied by the absolute value of the charge, so 1 mmol of Ca2+ is 2 mEq while 1 mmol of Na+ is 1 mEq. That is exactly what you want when you are balancing cations against anions in plasma. Mass is handled by grams and molar mass, osmotic pull by osmolarity, and movement rate by permeability, none of which the mEq unit encodes.

cards.q: Blood pressure is reported in mmHg. What does one mmHg represent?
cards.a: The pressure that will support a column of mercury 1 mm high.
options: The mass of a 1 mm column of mercury in milligrams
The volume of mercury displaced by one milliliter of blood
The force in newtons delivered over one square millimeter
The pressure that will support a column of mercury 1 mm high
cards.explanation: The unit comes straight from the mercury manometer: the pressure in the vessel is read off as the height of mercury it can hold up. A mass in milligrams is not a pressure, since pressure is force spread over an area. Displaced volume describes a different measurement entirely. Newtons per square millimeter is a genuine pressure unit but a much larger one, and it is not what the mercury column defines.

cards.q: An IV bag is labeled 0.9 percent NaCl. What does that percent tell you?
cards.a: It contains 0.9 grams of NaCl in every 100 mL of solution.
options: 0.9 grams of NaCl in every 100 mL of solution
0.9 grams of NaCl in every liter of solution
0.9 moles of NaCl in every 100 mL of solution
0.9 milligrams of NaCl in every milliliter of solution
cards.explanation: A percent solution in clinical use is weight per volume: grams of solute in 100 mL of solution. Grams per liter would be ten times too dilute, since 0.9 percent is 9 g/L. Moles per 100 mL would be a wildly concentrated solution, roughly 9 M. Milligrams per milliliter is the same as grams per liter, so 0.9 mg/mL is also ten times too dilute; the correct figure is 9 mg/mL.

cards.q: In which units is cardiac output reported?
cards.a: Liters per minute.
options: Milliliters per beat
Millimeters of mercury
Liters per minute
Beats per minute
cards.explanation: Cardiac output is a flow, a volume of blood ejected per unit time, so its units must be volume over time. Milliliters per beat is stroke volume, the volume of one ejection. Millimeters of mercury is a pressure, not a flow. Beats per minute is heart rate, and multiplying it by stroke volume is precisely how you arrive at liters per minute.

cards.q: One mole of NaCl dissolves completely in water. How many osmoles of particles does it produce?
cards.a: Two osmoles.
options: One osmole
Two osmoles
Three osmoles
Half an osmole
cards.explanation: NaCl separates into one Na+ and one Cl- in solution, and osmolarity counts particles, so one mole yields two osmoles. One osmole would be right for a solute that stays intact, such as glucose or urea. Three osmoles fits a salt that releases three particles, such as CaCl2. Half an osmole would require particles to combine in solution, which does not happen with a fully dissociating salt.

cards.q: A bag of 0.9 percent NaCl is hanging at the bedside. How many grams of NaCl does one liter of it contain?
cards.a: 9 grams.
options: 0.9 grams
9 grams
90 grams
0.09 grams
cards.explanation: Percent solutions are grams per 100 mL, and a liter is ten of those, so 0.9 g times 10 gives 9 g/L. Answering 0.9 g means reading the percent as grams per liter and skipping the conversion. 90 g multiplies by 100 instead of 10, which would be the answer if percent meant grams per 10 mL. 0.09 g divides where you should multiply.

cards.q: Normal saline is 154 mmol/L NaCl and NaCl dissociates completely. What is its approximate osmolarity?
cards.a: About 308 mOsm/L.
options: 77 mOsm/L
154 mOsm/L
231 mOsm/L
308 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Each NaCl gives two particles, so 154 mmol/L becomes 308 mOsm/L, which is why saline sits close to plasma at about 290 mOsm/L. Answering 154 treats NaCl as if it stayed intact in solution. 77 halves instead of doubling, the mistake you get from dividing by the number of ions. 231 would follow from assuming only half the NaCl dissociates, but dissociation of NaCl in dilute solution is essentially complete.

cards.q: Plasma calcium is reported as 2.5 mmol/L. What is that concentration in mEq/L?
cards.a: 5 mEq/L.
options: 1.25 mEq/L
2.5 mEq/L
5 mEq/L
10 mEq/L
cards.explanation: Milliequivalents equal millimoles times the charge number, and Ca2+ carries two charges, so 2.5 mmol/L is 5 mEq/L. Answering 2.5 treats calcium as though it were monovalent like Na+ or K+. 1.25 divides by the charge instead of multiplying. 10 multiplies by four, which would suit an ion carrying four charges, and none of the physiologically important ions do.

cards.q: Dry air is 21 percent oxygen and barometric pressure at sea level is 760 mmHg. What is the partial pressure of oxygen in dry inspired air?
cards.a: About 160 mmHg.
options: 100 mmHg
150 mmHg
160 mmHg
210 mmHg
cards.explanation: A partial pressure is the fractional concentration times the total pressure, so 0.21 times 760 gives about 160 mmHg. 150 mmHg is the value after the airway humidifies the air, which first subtracts the 47 mmHg of water vapor from 760. 100 mmHg is arterial PO2 after gas exchange in the alveoli, several steps further along. 210 mmHg comes from treating 21 percent as 210 mmHg directly and ignoring the barometric pressure.

cards.q: A resting subject has a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. What is the cardiac output?
cards.a: 4.9 L/min.
options: 4.9 L/min
0.49 L/min
9.8 L/min
49 L/min
cards.explanation: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume: 70 times 70 is 4900 mL/min, and 4900 mL is 4.9 L, right in the normal resting range. 49 L/min and 0.49 L/min are decimal slips of ten in each direction and neither is compatible with life at rest. 9.8 L/min doubles the correct value, which is what you get by adding an extra factor of two rather than converting milliliters to liters.

cards.q: A fasting plasma glucose is reported as 90 mg/dL. There are 10 deciliters in a liter. What is that concentration in mg/L?
options: 9 mg/L
90 mg/L
900 mg/L
cards.explanation: A liter holds ten deciliters, so multiply by ten: 90 mg/dL is 900 mg/L, or 0.9 g/L. Answering 90 leaves the number unchanged and treats a deciliter as a liter. 9 mg/L divides by ten instead of multiplying. 9000 mg/L multiplies by 100, which would be right only if there were 100 deciliters in a liter.

cards.q: A 5 percent dextrose solution contains 50 grams of dextrose per liter. Dextrose has a molar mass of 180 g/mol and does not dissociate. What is its approximate osmolarity?
cards.a: About 278 mOsm/L.
options: 90 mOsm/L
278 mOsm/L
556 mOsm/L
139 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Divide grams per liter by molar mass to get molarity: 50 divided by 180 is about 0.278 mol/L, and because dextrose stays as a single particle that is also 278 mOsm/L, close to plasma. 556 mOsm/L doubles as though the sugar dissociated the way a salt does, which it does not. 139 mOsm/L halves for the same mistaken reason in reverse. 90 mOsm/L would follow from using the 5 percent figure directly instead of the 50 g/L it represents.

cards.q: A red blood cell is dropped into a 300 mOsm/L solution of urea, a solute that crosses the cell membrane freely. Plasma osmolarity is also about 300 mOsm/L. What happens to the cell and why?
cards.a: It swells and can lyse, because urea enters the cell and water follows.
options: It swells and can lyse, because urea enters and water follows it in
It holds its volume, because the two osmolarities are equal
It shrinks, because urea draws water out of the cell
It holds its volume, because urea cannot cross the membrane
cards.explanation: The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic: urea equilibrates across the membrane, so it exerts no lasting osmotic pull, and the cell's impermeant solutes then draw water in. Saying the cell holds its volume because the osmolarities match is the classic error of treating osmolarity and tonicity as the same thing. Shrinkage would require a solute that stays outside and outnumbers the cell's own particles. Urea does cross the membrane readily, which is the whole point of the setup.

cards.q: An IV bag is labeled 0.45 percent NaCl. NaCl has a molar mass of about 58.5 g/mol and dissociates completely. Work out the osmolarity and predict the effect on red blood cells.
cards.a: About 154 mOsm/L, which is hypotonic, so the cells swell.
options: About 77 mOsm/L, so the cells shrink
About 154 mOsm/L, so the cells shrink
About 308 mOsm/L, so the cells hold their volume
About 154 mOsm/L, so the cells swell
cards.explanation: Work it in order: 0.45 percent is 4.5 g/L, divided by 58.5 g/mol gives about 0.077 mol/L, and doubling for the two ions gives roughly 154 mOsm/L. That is about half of plasma at 290 mOsm/L, so water moves into the cells and they swell. Shrinking would require a solution above plasma osmolarity. 308 mOsm/L is full strength normal saline at 0.9 percent, twice the concentration on this label, and 77 mOsm/L is the millimolar NaCl figure before the two ions are counted.

cards.q: During a treadmill test a subject's heart rate rises from 60 to 90 beats per minute while stroke volume falls from 80 mL to 60 mL. What happens to cardiac output?
cards.a: It rises from 4.8 to 5.4 L/min.
options: It falls from 4.8 to 4.2 L/min
It is unchanged at 4.8 L/min
It rises from 4.8 to 5.4 L/min
It rises from 4.8 to 7.2 L/min
cards.explanation: Multiply each pair: 60 times 80 is 4800 mL/min, or 4.8 L/min, and 90 times 60 is 5400 mL/min, or 5.4 L/min, so output rises even though stroke volume dropped. 7.2 L/min comes from applying the new heart rate to the old stroke volume and forgetting that stroke volume changed. Saying it is unchanged assumes the two changes cancel exactly, which they would only if rate and volume moved by the same factor. A fall would require the drop in stroke volume to outweigh the rise in rate, and here it does not.

cards.q: A lab makes a solution containing NaCl at 140 mmol/L plus glucose at 5 mmol/L. NaCl dissociates completely and glucose does not. What is the total osmolarity?
cards.a: About 285 mOsm/L.
options: 145 mOsm/L
285 mOsm/L
290 mOsm/L
150 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Handle each solute by its own particle count and then add: NaCl gives 140 times 2, or 280 mOsm/L, and glucose gives 5 mOsm/L, for 285 mOsm/L in total. 145 mOsm/L adds the millimolar figures without doubling the salt. 290 mOsm/L doubles the glucose too, which no nondissociating sugar does. 150 mOsm/L drops the glucose contribution and mishandles the salt at the same time.

cards.q: When you construct a graph of experimental data, which variable belongs on the x axis?
cards.a: The variable the experimenter set or manipulated, the independent variable.
options: The variable measured as the outcome
The variable that showed the largest change
The variable the experimenter set or manipulated
The variable held constant in every trial
cards.explanation: The x axis carries the independent variable, the one you chose the values for, so the graph reads left to right as cause then effect. The measured outcome is the dependent variable and belongs on the y axis. Size of change has nothing to do with axis placement. A variable held constant does not appear on either axis, because it has only one value and would plot as a single point.

cards.q: Where does the dependent variable belong on a properly constructed graph?
cards.a: On the y axis, the vertical axis.
options: On the y axis, the vertical axis
On the x axis, the horizontal axis
In the legend rather than on an axis
On either axis, as long as both are labeled
cards.explanation: The dependent variable is the response you measured, and by convention it goes on the vertical axis so that height reads as magnitude of the response. The x axis is reserved for the independent variable you controlled. A legend identifies which line is which when several conditions are plotted together, not which variable was measured. The convention is not optional, because a reader interprets slope as the change in the response per unit of the manipulated variable.

cards.q: On a graph with lung volume on the y axis and time on the x axis, what does the slope of the line represent?
cards.a: The rate at which volume is changing, that is, airflow.
options: The total volume of air moved during the trial
The volume present in the lungs at the start of the trace
The average volume across the whole recording
The rate at which volume is changing, that is, airflow
cards.explanation: Slope is the change on the y axis divided by the change on the x axis, so volume over time gives liters per second, which is flow. The total volume moved is read as the vertical distance between the start and the end of the trace, not its steepness. Starting volume is the y intercept. The average volume is a single summary height and carries no information about how fast air was moving.

cards.q: Besides the name of the variable, what must each axis of a physiology graph carry?
cards.a: The units in which the variable was measured.
options: The number of subjects tested
The units in which the variable was measured
The equation of the best fit line
The name of the instrument used
cards.explanation: Without units the numbers are meaningless: a pressure of 90 could be mmHg or kPa, and a volume of 3 could be liters or milliliters. Sample size, instrument, and any fitted equation belong in the figure caption or the methods, where a reader looks for them. An axis label is doing its job when someone can read a value off the graph and state it correctly with its unit.

cards.q: Which kind of graph fits an experiment in which the independent variable is continuous, such as time or temperature?
cards.a: A line graph.
options: A line graph
A bar graph
A pie chart
A stacked bar graph
cards.explanation: A continuous independent variable has meaningful values between the points you tested, so joining the points with a line correctly implies that the response varies smoothly in between. Bar graphs are for categories with nothing in between, such as three different muscles or three drug conditions. Pie charts show parts of a single whole, which is not what a dose response or a time course is. Stacked bars add components within categories and are a poor fit for continuous data as well.

cards.q: On a graph of a measured physiological response against a manipulated variable, what does the y intercept tell you?
cards.a: The value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero.
options: The largest value the dependent variable reached
The rate at which the dependent variable changed
The value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero
The point where the line crosses the horizontal axis
cards.explanation: The y intercept is the height of the line where x equals zero, which usually means the baseline or resting value before any treatment was applied. The rate of change is the slope, a separate feature of the same line. The maximum is simply the highest point plotted and often sits far from the intercept. The crossing of the horizontal axis is the x intercept, where the response reaches zero rather than where the treatment does.

cards.q: A plotted line has a negative slope. What is the relationship between the two variables?
cards.a: As the independent variable increases, the dependent variable decreases.
options: As the independent variable increases, the dependent variable also increases
The dependent variable does not change as the independent variable changes
The dependent variable changes faster at high values than at low values
As the independent variable increases, the dependent variable decreases
cards.explanation: A negative slope means the line falls from left to right, so every step up in the manipulated variable brings a step down in the measured response. Both increasing together would be a positive slope. No change at all would be a flat line with a slope of zero. Changing faster at high values describes a curve that steepens, which is about how the slope varies, not about its sign.

cards.q: A physiological curve rises steeply and then flattens into a plateau. What does the plateau region indicate?
cards.a: Further increases in the independent variable produce little or no further change in the response.
options: The response has begun falling back toward its baseline value
Further increases in the independent variable produce little further change
The recording instrument has stopped collecting data from the preparation
The independent variable has begun to decrease during the recording
cards.explanation: A plateau is a slope near zero, so the system has reached a maximum: transporters are saturated, all motor units are recruited, or hemoglobin is nearly fully bound. A fall back toward baseline would show as a downward slope, not a flat one. Instrument failure would give a flat line at zero or a broken trace, not a flat line at a high response value. The independent variable keeps rising across a plateau; that is exactly what makes the flatness informative.

cards.q: On the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve, percent saturation is plotted against PO2. Between a PO2 of 80 and 100 mmHg the curve is nearly flat. What does that slope tell you?
cards.a: A drop in alveolar PO2 within that range changes saturation very little.
options: Saturation falls steeply if alveolar PO2 drops anywhere in that range
A drop in alveolar PO2 within that range changes saturation very little
Hemoglobin unloads most of its oxygen to tissue in that range
Saturation and PO2 are unrelated at every PO2 on the curve
cards.explanation: A near zero slope means a large change in x buys almost no change in y, which is why moderate lung disease or modest altitude can lower alveolar PO2 without dropping arterial saturation much. A steep fall in that range would contradict the flatness described. Unloading happens on the steep part of the curve, at tissue PO2 values near 20 to 40 mmHg, where a small pressure drop releases a lot of oxygen. The variables are strongly related overall; the relationship simply flattens at high PO2.

cards.q: A spirometer plots expired volume in liters on the y axis against time in seconds. A student wants to report airflow. What should she take from the trace?
cards.a: The slope of the trace, which comes out in liters per second.
options: The slope of the trace, which comes out in liters per second
The highest point reached on the trace, in liters
The area beneath the trace, in liter seconds
The time from the start to the highest point, in seconds
cards.explanation: Flow is volume per unit time, and dividing the y units by the x units is exactly what a slope does, so the steepness of the trace is the flow. The highest point is the total volume expired, a volume rather than a flow. Area under a volume trace has units of liter seconds and no useful physiological meaning here. The time to peak tells you how long the effort took, not how fast air moved at any moment.

cards.q: You record core body temperature every two hours for 24 hours to look for a daily rhythm. How should the graph be built?
cards.a: Time on the x axis, temperature on the y axis, drawn as a line graph.
options: Temperature on the x axis, time on the y axis, as a line graph
Time on the x axis, temperature on the y axis, as a pie chart
Temperature on the x axis, time on the y axis, as a bar graph
Time on the x axis, temperature on the y axis, as a line graph
cards.explanation: Time is the independent variable here, since you chose the sampling schedule and did not set the temperature, so time goes on x and the measured temperature on y. Putting temperature on x reverses the roles and makes the rhythm impossible to read. A pie chart divides a whole into parts and cannot show a time course at all. A bar graph would also be wrong because time is continuous and the reader should be able to interpolate between samples.

cards.q: A nerve is stimulated at several distances from the recording electrode, and each greater distance gives a longer latency. Distance in millimeters is plotted on the y axis against latency in milliseconds on the x axis. What does the slope give you?
cards.a: The conduction velocity, in millimeters per millisecond.
options: The refractory period, in milliseconds
The threshold for firing, in millivolts
The conduction velocity, in millimeters per millisecond
The total conduction time, in milliseconds
cards.explanation: Slope is the y change over the x change, so millimeters divided by milliseconds is a speed, and that speed is conduction velocity. The refractory period comes from paired stimuli at varying intervals, not from distance and latency. Threshold is found by raising stimulus strength until a response appears and is measured in millivolts, a different axis pair entirely. Total conduction time is a single x value read off the graph, not the steepness of the line.

cards.q: In a muscle lab, stimulus frequency is raised from 5 to 50 Hz and twitch tension rises steeply at first, then levels off near the top of the range. Which description of the trend is accurate?
cards.a: A rise that saturates, so added frequency buys progressively less tension.
options: A steady linear rise of the same steepness across the whole range
A steady fall in tension that levels off at higher frequencies
A rise that saturates, so added frequency buys progressively less tension
No consistent relationship between frequency and tension
cards.explanation: The slope is steep early and near zero late, which is the shape of summation moving into fused tetanus: once calcium stays elevated between stimuli, extra stimuli add almost nothing. A linear rise would keep the same slope from 5 to 50 Hz, which the described flattening rules out. A fall would mean tension decreasing with frequency, the opposite of what was recorded. There is clearly a relationship, just a nonlinear one.

cards.q: You compare mean strength recorded from three different muscle groups: hand, forearm, and biceps. Which graph presents this best?
cards.a: A bar graph, because the independent variable is a set of categories.
options: A line graph, because muscle strength is a continuous measurement
A bar graph, because the independent variable is a set of categories
A pie chart, because three groups are being compared to each other
A line graph, because there are only three points to connect
cards.explanation: Graph type is decided by the independent variable, and muscle group is categorical with nothing meaningful between hand and forearm, so bars are correct. The dependent variable being continuous does not license a line, since a line would falsely suggest a value halfway between two muscles. A pie chart would imply the three strengths are parts of one total, which they are not. Having only three points is not a reason either way.

cards.q: Heart rate rises from 70 to 130 beats per minute as cycling workload rises from 0 to 120 watts, and the points fall on a straight line. What is the slope?
cards.a: 0.5 beats per minute per watt.
options: 0.5 beats per minute per watt
2 beats per minute per watt
60 beats per minute per watt
0.5 watts per beat per minute
cards.explanation: Slope is the rise over the run: 130 minus 70 is 60 beats per minute, divided by 120 watts, giving 0.5 beats per minute per watt. Answering 2 divides the workload by the heart rate change and inverts the calculation. Answering 60 reports the rise alone and never divides by the run. The last option has the right number but the units upside down, which would describe watts per heartbeat rather than the response per unit of work.

cards.q: Heart rate is plotted against workload for one subject on two days. On the control day the line starts at 70 beats per minute at rest with a slope of 0.5 beats per minute per watt. After a beta blocker the line starts at 55 with a slope of 0.25. What do the two lines together show?
cards.a: The drug lowered resting heart rate and also blunted the rise with workload.
options: The drug lowered resting heart rate but left the response to work unchanged
The drug raised resting heart rate and blunted the response to work
The drug left resting heart rate unchanged and only blunted the response to work
The drug lowered resting heart rate and also blunted the rise with workload
cards.explanation: Read the two features separately: the intercept fell from 70 to 55, which is the resting effect, and the slope halved from 0.5 to 0.25, which is the reduced responsiveness to sympathetic drive during work. Saying the response to work is unchanged ignores the change in slope. Saying resting rate is unchanged ignores the change in intercept. Nothing rose, so the option describing a higher resting rate contradicts the intercepts given.

cards.q: Glucose reabsorption by the kidney is plotted on the y axis against plasma glucose on the x axis. The line rises straight, then bends, then runs flat. What does the flat portion mean?
cards.a: The reabsorptive transporters are saturated, so more plasma glucose adds no more reabsorption.
options: The glomerulus has stopped filtering glucose at those plasma levels
The transporters are saturated, so more plasma glucose adds no more reabsorption
Glucose has begun moving from the blood back into the tubule
Plasma glucose has stopped rising, so reabsorption cannot rise either
cards.explanation: A flat region means the slope has fallen to zero: every carrier is occupied, so raising the load no longer raises the amount reabsorbed, and that ceiling is the transport maximum. Filtration keeps climbing with plasma glucose, which is why the excess spills into the urine rather than disappearing. Movement back into the tubule would show as a falling line, not a flat one. Plasma glucose is the x variable and by construction it keeps increasing across the flat region.

cards.q: A student graphs a spirometry trial with time on the y axis and volume on the x axis, then reports a slope of 0.4 seconds per liter. What is wrong and how should it be fixed?
cards.a: The axes are reversed, so the slope is the inverse of flow; replot with time on the x axis to get liters per second.
options: The axes are reversed, so the slope is the inverse of flow; replot with time on x
Nothing is wrong; seconds per liter describes the trial just as well as flow does
The slope is fine and the units can simply be relabeled liters per second
The data should be shown as bars, since two continuous variables cannot share a line
cards.explanation: Time is the independent variable and belongs on x, so with the axes swapped the slope came out as time per volume, the reciprocal of flow. Relabeling without replotting would attach the wrong units to the number, and 0.4 seconds per liter is 2.5 liters per second, not 0.4. It is true that the reciprocal contains the same information, but reporting a flow requires the conventional axes and the conventional units so that others can compare the value. A bar graph is wrong here because both variables are continuous and a line correctly implies the values in between.

cards.q: Two traces share one time axis. Mean arterial pressure runs flat at 90 mmHg, falls steadily to 60 mmHg over two minutes, then holds at 60. Heart rate sits at 70 beats per minute and climbs to 110 during the same two minutes. What do the traces show together?
cards.a: Pressure fell while heart rate rose, the reflex response to the falling pressure.
options: Pressure and heart rate both fell, so the heart slowed and output dropped
Pressure began to fall only after heart rate had returned to baseline
Pressure fell while heart rate rose, the reflex response to the falling pressure
Heart rate rose first and drove pressure down by shortening filling time
cards.explanation: Read the two slopes over the same interval: one is negative and one is positive, and they change together, which is the baroreceptor reflex responding to reduced stretch by raising heart rate. Both falling is simply not what the traces describe. Heart rate never returns to baseline in this record, so the second option misreads the timing. The last option reverses cause and effect, and a tachycardia driven by reflex is the compensation for the pressure drop rather than its source.

cards.q: In a physiology experiment, what is the independent variable?
cards.a: The variable the experimenter deliberately changes.
options: The variable measured as the outcome of the experiment
The variable the experimenter deliberately changes
The variable held constant across every group
The variable that differs between subjects by chance
cards.explanation: The independent variable is what you set: the dose, the temperature, the stimulus frequency, the workload. The measured outcome is the dependent variable, which is what you hope will respond. A variable held constant across groups is a controlled variable, deliberately prevented from varying. Differences that arise by chance between subjects are a source of variability you try to balance across groups, not a variable you manipulate.

cards.q: What is the dependent variable in an experiment?
cards.a: The response that is measured and may change with the treatment.
options: The condition the experimenter sets before the trial begins
Any factor kept the same across all of the groups
The group that receives no treatment at all
The response that is measured and may change with the treatment
cards.explanation: The dependent variable is the readout, the number you collect, and its name reflects that its value may depend on what you did to the independent variable. The condition you set in advance is the independent variable. Factors held the same across groups are controlled variables. The untreated group is the control condition, a group rather than a variable.

cards.q: What makes a condition a control in a physiology experiment?
cards.a: It is treated identically except for the one variable being tested.
options: It is treated identically except for the one variable being tested
It contains the largest number of subjects in the study
It is measured after all the other groups have been measured
It is the group in which the biggest change is expected
cards.explanation: A control works by being the same in every respect but one, so that any difference in the result can be traced to the single variable you changed. Group size matters for statistical power but does not make a group a control. Measurement order is a matter of scheduling and can even introduce a confound if all controls are run last. The control is normally where you expect little or no change, which is what makes a change in the treated group meaningful.

cards.q: Which statement is written as a testable hypothesis?
cards.a: Drinking 200 mg of caffeine raises resting heart rate in adults.
options: Caffeine is an interesting compound to study in a physiology lab
How does caffeine change resting heart rate in healthy adults?
Drinking 200 mg of caffeine raises resting heart rate in adults
Heart rate was measured before and after caffeine in ten adults
cards.explanation: A hypothesis is a declarative, falsifiable prediction that names the variables and the expected direction, so data can either support it or contradict it. The question form states what you want to know but predicts nothing, so no result could refute it. The statement about caffeine being interesting is an opinion and cannot be tested. The last option describes what was done, which is a method, not a prediction made in advance.

cards.q: A drug is dissolved in saline and injected into an animal. Why is a second group injected with saline alone?
cards.a: To separate the effect of the drug from the effect of the injection and the saline itself.
options: To increase the total number of animals in the study
To make sure both groups receive the same dose of drug
To confirm that the drug fully dissolved before injection
To separate the drug's effect from the effect of the injection and the saline
cards.explanation: This is a vehicle control: it delivers everything the treated group got except the active compound, so handling, needle stress, and the fluid volume are matched. Adding animals to boost numbers is not the purpose, and the saline group is not a source of extra treated data. Both groups obviously do not receive the same dose, since the point is that one gets none. Whether the drug dissolved is checked when the solution is prepared, not by injecting a second group.

cards.q: What are controlled variables in an experiment?
cards.a: Factors held the same in every group so they cannot explain the result.
options: Factors the experimenter measures as the outcome of the study
Factors held the same in every group so they cannot explain the result
Factors allowed to change freely during the experiment
Factors removed from the analysis once data collection ends
cards.explanation: Bath temperature, stimulus voltage, time of day, and posture are typical controlled variables: you hold them fixed so that any difference between groups points to the one variable you did manipulate. Measured outcomes are dependent variables. Factors allowed to change freely are exactly what a good design tries to prevent, because they become confounds. Dropping a variable during analysis does not undo its influence on the data already collected.

cards.q: In a human physiology study, what is a placebo?
cards.a: An inactive treatment that looks and feels like the real one.
options: A second dose of the active drug given later in the session
A dose so small that no measurable effect is expected
An inactive treatment that looks and feels like the real one
A measurement taken before any treatment has been given
cards.explanation: A placebo matches the treatment in appearance, taste, and delivery but contains no active agent, so any difference between groups cannot be attributed to expectation. A tiny dose of the real drug is still the real drug and would be a low dose arm, not a placebo. A repeat dose is part of the treatment schedule. A measurement taken before treatment is a baseline, useful but different, since it does not control for the subject's belief that something was given.

cards.q: What does a positive control demonstrate in an experiment?
cards.a: That the setup can detect an effect when one is truly present.
options: That the setup can detect an effect when one is truly present
That the treatment being tested produced a real effect
That no unexpected variables entered the experiment
That the results reached statistical significance
cards.explanation: A positive control is a condition known to produce the response, so if it comes out flat you know the method failed rather than concluding the treatment does nothing. It says nothing about the treatment under test, which is what the experimental group is for. Excluding unexpected variables is the job of controlled variables and randomization. Statistical significance is decided by the analysis of the data, not by any single control condition.

cards.q: Students give volunteers 0, 100, or 200 mg of caffeine and record resting heart rate 30 minutes later. What is the independent variable?
cards.a: The dose of caffeine given.
options: The resting heart rate recorded at the end
The 30 minute waiting period before measuring
The dose of caffeine given
The number of volunteers who took part
cards.explanation: The dose is the one thing set to different values by the team, which makes it the independent variable and puts it on the x axis. Resting heart rate is what they measured, so it is the dependent variable. The 30 minute wait is the same for everyone, which makes it a controlled variable rather than a manipulated one. Sample size is a feature of the study design, not a variable measured or manipulated within it.

cards.q: A frog heart in a dish beats steadily. Adding epinephrine dissolved in Ringer's solution speeds it up. A second heart receives an equal volume of plain Ringer's solution. What does that control rule out?
cards.a: That the added fluid, rather than the epinephrine, sped up the heart.
options: That the added fluid, rather than the epinephrine, sped up the heart
That epinephrine acts on beta receptors in cardiac tissue
That the recording equipment measures rate accurately
That the two hearts came from different frogs
cards.explanation: The plain Ringer's group receives everything except the hormone, so if those hearts do not speed up, the volume added, the temperature of the fluid, and the disturbance of pipetting are all eliminated as explanations. Which receptor epinephrine binds is answered by adding a blocker, not by a vehicle control. Instrument accuracy is settled by calibration before the experiment. Differences between the two frogs remain, which is why several hearts per condition are better than one.

cards.q: A subject squeezes a hand dynamometer once every two seconds until force falls below half of the starting value, and the team records force on every squeeze. What is the dependent variable?
cards.a: The force produced on each squeeze.
options: The two second interval between squeezes
The half maximal cutoff chosen in advance
The hand the subject used for squeezing
The force produced on each squeeze
cards.explanation: Force is the number being measured and the one expected to fall as the muscle fatigues, so it is the dependent variable. The squeeze interval is fixed by the protocol, making it a controlled variable. The half maximal cutoff is a stopping rule the team decided in advance rather than something measured. Which hand is used is also held constant, and if it were allowed to vary it would become a confound rather than a dependent variable.

cards.q: In a cold pressor test, one hand is placed in ice water for one minute while blood pressure is recorded every 15 seconds. Which is the dependent variable?
cards.a: The blood pressure recorded during the immersion.
options: The temperature of the ice water bath
The blood pressure recorded during the immersion
The one minute duration of the exposure
The hand chosen for immersion
cards.explanation: Blood pressure is what the team measures and what the cold stimulus is expected to change through sympathetic activation, so it is the dependent variable. The water temperature is the manipulated condition, the independent variable. The one minute exposure and the choice of hand are both fixed by the protocol, which makes them controlled variables that must be identical for every subject if the comparison is to mean anything.

cards.q: Rats given an insulin injection show a fall in blood glucose. A second group is handled the same way and injected with saline. What does the saline group allow the team to conclude?
cards.a: That the fall in glucose was not caused by handling and injection alone.
options: That insulin lowers glucose by acting on the liver
That the insulin dose used was the smallest effective dose
That blood glucose can be measured accurately in rats
That the fall in glucose was not caused by handling and injection alone
cards.explanation: Restraint and needle stick raise catecholamines and can move glucose on their own, so the saline group shows what handling by itself does and lets the team subtract it. Where insulin acts requires tissue level work such as measuring glucose uptake in muscle or liver. Finding the smallest effective dose requires several doses, not one dose plus saline. Assay accuracy is established with known standards, which is a calibration question rather than a control group question.

cards.q: A frog nerve preparation is tested at several stimulus voltages while the bath is held at 22 C throughout. What role does bath temperature play in this experiment?
cards.a: It is a controlled variable, held constant so it cannot explain the results.
options: It is a controlled variable, held constant so it cannot explain the results
It is the independent variable, since the team chose the value of 22 C
It is the dependent variable, since it was read from a thermometer
It is the control condition, since no stimulus is applied at 22 C
cards.explanation: Temperature strongly affects conduction, so holding it at one value keeps it from varying with voltage and confounding the result. Choosing a value is not the same as manipulating it: an independent variable must take more than one value across the experiment. It is not a dependent variable, because it is not free to respond to the treatment. A control condition is a group of preparations, not a single held constant, and stimuli are applied at 22 C in every trial here.

cards.q: A team plans to warm a frog nerve from 20 C to 30 C and measure conduction velocity. Which sentence is their hypothesis?
cards.a: Warming the nerve from 20 C to 30 C will increase conduction velocity.
options: Conduction velocity will be measured at both bath temperatures
Warming a nerve is a common procedure in physiology teaching labs
Warming the nerve from 20 C to 30 C will increase conduction velocity
Does warming a nerve change how fast it conducts an impulse?
cards.explanation: A hypothesis predicts a direction of change and names both variables, so the data can confirm or refute it. Stating that velocity will be measured at both temperatures describes the method and predicts nothing. The remark about teaching labs is background information. The question form identifies what the team wants to know but leaves no prediction to be wrong about, which is what separates a research question from a hypothesis.

cards.q: One group jogs outdoors on a hot afternoon while a comparison group sits in an air conditioned room. Heart rate is higher in the joggers, and the team concludes that exercise raises heart rate. Why is that conclusion unsafe from this design?
cards.a: Exercise and ambient temperature changed together, so either one could explain the difference.
options: Heart rate is not a valid measure of cardiovascular work during exercise
Exercise and ambient temperature changed together, so either could explain it
The seated group should also have jogged before their measurement was taken
Heart rate cannot be compared between two different groups of people
cards.explanation: Two variables moved at once, so the design cannot separate the effect of muscular work from the effect of heat, which raises heart rate on its own through skin vasodilation and sweating. The fix is to have both groups in the same environment and vary only the activity. Heart rate is a perfectly good measure here and is not the problem. Having the seated group jog would erase the comparison altogether. Groups of different people can be compared, provided the groups differ in only the one variable of interest.

cards.q: Conduction velocity is measured in a frog nerve, the bath is warmed from 20 C to 30 C over 20 minutes, and velocity is higher at the end. Which control would let the team credit the warming rather than the passage of time?
cards.a: A second nerve held at 20 C and measured on the same schedule.
options: A second nerve stimulated at a higher voltage from the start
A second nerve measured only once, at the end of the 20 minutes
A second nerve held at 20 C and measured on the same schedule
A second nerve warmed all the way to 40 C on the same schedule
cards.explanation: A preparation left sitting for 20 minutes can drift on its own as the tissue dries or recovers from dissection, so a time matched nerve at the starting temperature shows what that drift looks like with no warming at all. Measuring the second nerve only at the end gives no time course to compare against. Raising the voltage changes a different variable and answers a different question. Warming to 40 C extends the dose range, which is useful, but it still leaves time and temperature moving together.

cards.q: A muscle preparation is stimulated once a minute for an hour. A fatigue inducing drug is added at minute 30 and force declines steadily afterward. No untreated preparation was run alongside. What can the team honestly conclude?
cards.a: Very little, because a preparation stimulated for an hour weakens on its own.
options: The drug caused the decline, since force fell only after it was added
The drug had no effect, since the preparation was already failing anyway
The drug caused the decline, since the stimulus was never changed
Very little, because a preparation stimulated for an hour weakens on its own
cards.explanation: Time and drug are confounded: an isolated muscle run down over an hour of stimulation whether or not anything is added, so the second half of the record cannot be assigned to the drug. A parallel preparation stimulated on the same schedule with no drug would supply the missing comparison. The two options that credit the drug both rest on timing alone, which is exactly the reasoning the missing control was supposed to check. Concluding no effect is equally unsupported, since the data cannot separate the two possibilities in either direction.

cards.q: An enzyme assay returns no signal in the treated samples. The positive control, a sample known to contain the enzyme, also returns no signal. What is the right conclusion?
cards.a: The assay itself failed, so the treated samples cannot be interpreted.
options: The assay itself failed, so the treated samples cannot be interpreted
The treatment destroyed the enzyme in the samples and the control alike
The enzyme is absent from the treated samples, just as the data show
The negative control was contaminated and absorbed the missing signal
cards.explanation: A positive control exists to prove the method can produce a signal, and when it comes back blank the whole run is uninterpretable, most often because a reagent expired or a step was skipped. Reading the treated samples as truly enzyme free is the trap here, since you cannot distinguish absent enzyme from an assay that never worked. The treatment was not applied to the positive control, so it cannot explain that sample's failure. A contaminated negative control would produce extra signal somewhere, not remove signal from another tube.

cards.q: What is random error in a physiological measurement?
cards.a: Unpredictable scatter that pushes readings above and below the true value.
options: An error that shifts every reading in the same direction
A mistake in the arithmetic used to analyze the collected data
A real change in the variable that is being measured
Unpredictable scatter that pushes readings above and below the true value
cards.explanation: Random error has no preferred direction, so repeated readings straddle the true value and their mean converges on it as trials accumulate. An error that always shifts one way is systematic and averaging will never remove it. An arithmetic mistake is a blunder, correctable by rechecking rather than by repeating the measurement. A real change in the variable is biological signal, not error, even though it also makes the numbers move.

cards.q: What is systematic error?
cards.a: A consistent bias that shifts every reading in the same direction.
options: Scatter that is equally likely to fall high or low on any given trial
A consistent bias that shifts every reading in the same direction
A single mistyped value entered into the data table
Normal biological variation from one subject to the next
cards.explanation: Systematic error is a bias built into the instrument or the technique, such as a transducer with an offset or a cuff of the wrong size, and it moves every reading the same way by roughly the same amount. Scatter with no preferred direction is random error. A mistyped value is a one time recording mistake rather than a property of the method. Variation between subjects is real physiology and belongs in the analysis, not in the error budget of the instrument.

cards.q: Repeating a measurement many times and averaging mainly reduces which problem?
cards.a: Random scatter among repeated readings, that is, random error.
options: Random scatter among repeated readings
Systematic bias built into the instrument
True biological variation between different subjects
An incorrect choice of dependent variable
cards.explanation: Random deviations are as likely to be high as low, so they partly cancel in a mean, and the more trials you average the closer the mean sits to the true value. A built in bias survives averaging untouched, because it pushes every trial the same way. Variation between subjects is not removed by repeating measurements on one subject, and it is often the thing you actually want to describe. Choosing the wrong dependent variable is a design flaw that no amount of repetition will repair.

cards.q: What does accuracy describe in a measurement?
cards.a: How close a reading is to the true value.
options: How closely repeated readings agree with one another
How many decimal places the instrument displays
How close a reading is to the true value
How quickly the instrument produces a reading
cards.explanation: Accuracy is about truth: an accurate blood pressure reading matches what an arterial line would show. Agreement among repeats is precision, and an instrument can be beautifully precise while consistently wrong. Displayed decimal places are resolution, and adding digits to a biased reading does not bring it closer to the truth. Speed of measurement is a practical property with no bearing on either accuracy or precision.

cards.q: What does precision describe?
cards.a: How closely repeated measurements agree with one another.
options: How closely repeated measurements agree with one another
How close the average reading is to the true value
How wide a range of values the instrument can measure
How well the instrument resists a built in bias
cards.explanation: Precision is repeatability: three heart rate counts of 70, 70, and 71 are precise whether or not 70 is the true rate. Closeness of the average to the truth is accuracy, and the two properties are independent, which is why calibration and repetition solve different problems. The span of measurable values is the instrument's range. Resistance to bias is again an accuracy question, addressed by calibrating against a known standard.

cards.q: Why is a pressure transducer calibrated against a known pressure before a lab session?
cards.a: To reveal and correct a consistent offset in its readings.
options: To reduce the scatter among repeated readings from the same subject
To confirm that the subject is fully at rest before recording begins
To increase the number of readings that can be collected per minute
To reveal and correct a consistent offset in its readings
cards.explanation: Calibration compares the instrument against a value you already know, which exposes any fixed offset or scaling error and lets you correct it before the data matter. Scatter among repeats is random error and is handled by averaging, not by calibration. Whether the subject is at rest is checked by watching a stable baseline, a separate step. Sampling rate is a setting on the recorder and has nothing to do with the calibration procedure.

cards.q: A blood pressure cuff reads exactly 8 mmHg higher than a calibrated reference on every one of ten trials. What kind of error is this?
cards.a: Systematic error, because the bias is the same size and direction each time.
options: Random error, because 8 mmHg is a small difference in clinical terms
Random error, because blood pressure varies from beat to beat anyway
Systematic error, because the bias is the same size and direction each time
Systematic error, because the readings scatter around the true value
cards.explanation: Consistency in size and direction is the signature of a systematic error, and the fix is calibration or a corrected cuff, not more trials. Random error would put some readings above the reference and some below. The size of the difference does not determine its type, so a small consistent offset is still systematic. The last option gives the right label with the wrong reason: scattering around the true value describes random error, not bias.

cards.q: Three resting heart rate counts on the same subject give 68, 72, and 70 beats per minute. How should the result be reported and why?
cards.a: As 70, the mean of the three, since averaging cancels random counting error.
options: As 72, since the highest count is the least likely to have missed a beat
As 70, the mean of the three, since averaging cancels random counting error
As 68, since the lowest count best reflects a truly resting state
As a range of 68 to 72, since no single value can be defended
cards.explanation: The three values scatter above and below a central figure with no consistent direction, which is random error, and the mean of 70 is the best single estimate of the true rate. Choosing the highest or the lowest deliberately introduces a bias in one direction and throws away two thirds of the data. Reporting the range is honest about the spread and is worth including alongside the mean, but a range alone is not the estimate the competency asks for.

cards.q: Why do physiology labs record several trials and average them rather than trusting a single reading?
cards.a: Because random fluctuations partly cancel, so the mean sits closer to the true value.
options: Because taking more trials makes the instrument itself more accurate
Because averaging removes any bias built into the measuring device
Because a single reading is always wrong by a large amount
Because random fluctuations partly cancel, so the mean sits closer to the truth
cards.explanation: Averaging works on random error, whose deviations are as likely to be positive as negative, so the mean of several trials is a better estimate than any one of them. The instrument is unchanged by how many times you use it, so it does not become more accurate. A built in bias shifts every trial the same way and survives averaging completely. A single reading is not always badly wrong, it is simply less reliable than a mean, and you have no way to know from one value how far off it is.

cards.q: A cuff that is too small for a subject's arm gives blood pressure readings that are consistently too high. Will averaging more readings fix the problem?
cards.a: No, because every reading carries the same upward bias.
options: No, because every reading carries the same upward bias
Yes, because averaging removes measurement error of every kind
Yes, because the bias will cancel out over enough repeated trials
No, because blood pressure changes too quickly to be averaged at all
cards.explanation: An undersized cuff must be squeezed harder to compress the artery, so every reading is shifted up by a similar amount and the mean of many biased readings is just as biased. The fix is a correctly sized cuff, which is a calibration of technique rather than a statistical remedy. Averaging removes only random error, not bias, so both of the yes options mistake one type of error for the other. Blood pressure does fluctuate, but that fluctuation is precisely what averaging handles well.

cards.q: Continuous recording shows heart rate rising slightly with each inhalation and falling with each exhalation. Is this measurement error?
cards.a: No, it is real biological variation in the subject.
options: Yes, it is random error arising from the recording electrodes
No, it is real biological variation in the subject
Yes, it is a systematic error introduced by the act of breathing
No, it is an artifact that the analysis software should remove
cards.explanation: This is respiratory sinus arrhythmia, a genuine vagal effect on the sinoatrial node, so the instrument is reporting the truth and the variation is signal rather than noise. Electrode noise would appear as irregular spikes unrelated to the breathing cycle. Calling it systematic error mislabels a real physiological rhythm as instrument bias. Filtering it out would discard a finding students are often asked to demonstrate, which is why the right move is to report it and note the breathing pattern.

cards.q: Two students measure the same subject's grip strength on two different dynamometers. Student A's readings average 40 kg and student B's average 35 kg, and each student's own three trials agree within 1 kg. What does this pattern indicate, and what would test it?
cards.a: A consistent offset between the instruments; hanging a known weight on each would reveal it.
options: Random error in both instruments, so each student should take more trials
Real variation in the subject, so the two should measure on separate days
A consistent offset between the instruments; hang a known weight on each
Poor precision in both instruments, so both dynamometers should be replaced
cards.explanation: Each device is precise, since its own repeats agree within 1 kg, yet the two disagree by 5 kg, and that combination points squarely at a systematic offset in at least one instrument. Testing them against a known weight tells you which one is off and by how much. More trials cannot help, because averaging does nothing to a fixed bias. The tight spread within each set rules out poor precision, and true fluctuation in the subject would show up as scatter within a student's own trials as well.

cards.q: A pulse oximeter on a finger with dark nail polish reads 91 percent while an arterial blood sample drawn at the same moment shows 98 percent saturation. Repeated oximeter readings agree within 1 percent. What is going on?
cards.a: A systematic error caused by the polish, so more readings will not correct it.
options: A systematic error caused by the polish, so more readings will not correct it
A random error, so averaging ten readings would bring the value to 98 percent
A true fall in saturation occurring between the two measurements
Poor precision in the oximeter, which the arterial sample has now confirmed
cards.explanation: The polish absorbs some of the light the oximeter shines through the finger, biasing every reading downward by a similar amount, and the tight agreement among repeats confirms the device is precise but inaccurate. Removing the polish or moving the probe to another site is the fix, not more trials, since averaging touches only random error. The two measurements were simultaneous, so a real change in saturation cannot explain the gap. Precision is clearly good here, which is what makes the disagreement with the arterial sample so telling.

cards.q: Reaction times for one subject scatter from 180 to 320 ms across 20 trials, with a mean of 240 ms. A classmate performs one trial, gets 195 ms, and claims to be faster. What is the sound conclusion?
cards.a: One trial cannot support the claim, because a single value can land anywhere in the scatter.
options: The classmate is faster, since 195 ms is well below the 240 ms mean
The classmate is slower, since 195 ms falls inside the first subject's range
Neither subject can be compared, since reaction time is a systematic error
One trial cannot support the claim, since a single value can land anywhere
cards.explanation: Reaction time carries large random variation, and 195 ms sits comfortably inside the first subject's own range of 180 to 320 ms, so a single draw from a wide distribution says almost nothing about which mean is lower. The classmate needs a comparable set of trials so the two means can be compared. Falling inside the range does not make the classmate slower either, since one value cannot establish a direction in either direction. Reaction time is a measured variable with random variation, not a systematic error.
